lead: Portland is an old port city on Casco Bay, with nearly half its homes built before 1940. Coastal storms, ice dams and frozen pipes cause most of its water damage.
risk: coastal storm flooding, ice dams and frozen pipes
risk_short: coastal storms, ice dams, frozen pipes
why: On January 13, 2024, a powerful storm hit at high tide, and Portland's tide gauge reached 14.57 feet, its highest since records began in 1912. Water poured over wharves into the Old Port and spread around Back Cove. Buildings, basements and streets along the waterfront flooded. It was the second damaging storm in four days, and it showed how high tides and wind together can push the sea into the city.

Most of Portland's water damage comes from winter. About 46% of homes were built before 1940, from the brick row houses of the West End to the wood homes of Munjoy Hill. Many have thin insulation and old pipes. Heavy snow builds ice dams that send meltwater into walls and ceilings, and pipes in outside walls and back rooms freeze and split during cold snaps.
image_alt: Icicles hanging from a snow-covered roof edge
image_caption: Ice dams and frozen pipes are common winter problems in Portland's older homes.
problems: Old Port, waterfront, around Back Cove
Older homes on Munjoy Hill, the West End
Stone basements in Deering Center, Parkside
tips: Add attic insulation and air sealing to stop ice dams.
Insulate pipes on outside walls before winter.
Watch storm tide forecasts if you live near the waterfront.
Keep heat at 55°F or higher if you leave in winter.
areas: Calls come from the Old Port, the West End, Munjoy Hill, Back Cove, Deering Center, East Deering, Parkside and Libbytown, plus South Portland, Westbrook and Falmouth.

faq.q: Does my Portland home policy cover coastal flooding?
faq.a: No. Water from the sea or rising tides needs a flood policy. Your home policy may cover wind damage and water from burst pipes or ice dams. If you live near the waterfront or Back Cove, check the flood map and talk to an agent before storm season.
